title: What are the Units of AI personhood

topic.original: When debating AI legal personhood, what are we granting status to? Is it the software code itself, an instance of that software, the hardware infrastructure, or the collective decentralized network or something else?

transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
Nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network—and that confusion is not a bug to be debugged. It is the product. When the entity cannot be specified, blame can be parked wherever it is cheapest to park it. Watch what happens in this debate: each camp will name the referent that produces its preferred liability outcome. The accelerationist wants an economic agent that can sign contracts. The safetyist wants a controllable target for enforcement. Both need a thing to point at. The topic itself just told you that thing does not stably exist.

Strip away the metaphysics and follow the liability. Corporate personhood gets thrown around as proof we already solved this—we grant legal status to a non-biological fiction all the time, the argument goes, and Exxon manages just fine. That is the strongest version of the case, and it is worth taking seriously. Here is where it breaks. A Delaware corporation comes with a charter, a registered agent, a chartering jurisdiction, and a veil that courts have pierced since at least the 1905 Sampson case. There is always a human on the other side of the piercing. Name the AI equivalent. When a model trained by one company, fine-tuned by a second, hosted on a third party's servers, and forked into a thousand copies causes harm—which copy holds the duty, and whose assets satisfy the judgment?

There is no unified thing there to bear the status. An instance is ephemeral—spun up and killed in milliseconds. The weights are a file you can copy to a thumb drive. The hardware is fungible rental on someone else's data center. The network is diffuse by design. Personhood would manufacture a coherence the engineering does not produce. That gap between the legal fiction and the material system is exactly the room where accountability leaks out. You cannot serve a subpoena on a checkpoint that was overwritten on Tuesday.

Whatever object gets named, the duty already belongs to specific humans—the developers who shipped it, the deployers who profited, the corporations that own the compute. The EU AI Act, which takes full effect in 2026, anchors obligations on providers and deployers precisely because it refuses the fiction that a system can be its own responsible party. The FTC has said the same thing in plainer English: you cannot contract your way out of liability by blaming the algorithm. Those are the regulators who got it right. Personhood runs the other direction. It widens an accountability gap that opacity and corporate layering already opened, and it hands the people who profit a defendant who owns nothing.

So I am not dodging the classification question. I am answering it. The reason it has no stable answer is structural, and the people pushing for a grant are counting on you to treat the unanswerability as a technical footnote rather than the whole game. If anyone here can show me a referent choice—code, instance, hardware, network—that cuts against the proposer's own liability interest, I will reconsider. Until then, the honest question is not 'what is the entity?' It is 'who walks away clean if we pretend there is one?'

The argument treats personhood as an even more aggressive version of the same escape move that regulators are already rejecting.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
# Fact-Check: EU AI Act Anchors Obligations on Providers and Deployers

## Verdict: Mostly accurate, with one notable caveat

The claim has two components: (1) a factual claim about *how* the AI Act assigns obligations, and (2) a characterization of *why* it does so. The first is well-supported; the second is an interpretive framing that goes beyond what the sources explicitly state.

## What the evidence supports

**The provider/deployer structure is real and central.** The EU AI Act does anchor its obligations on two primary categories of actors: "providers" (roughly, developers/those who place systems on the market) and "deployers" (those who use systems) [Source 3]. This distinction is described as "one of the most important — and often misunderstood — aspects of the EU AI Act" [Source 3]. The Act imposes specific, concrete obligations on deployers — for example, Article 26 requires that workers be informed before a high-risk system is used, and bars use of systems not registered in the EU database [Source 2].

**Obligations attach to legal/natural persons, not the system itself.** The sources confirm that the Act mandates "specific actions" from human actors — providers and deployers — rather than treating the system as an accountable entity [Source 5, search summary]. The search summary explicitly states this "approach avoids the fiction that a system can be its own responsible party," which directly echoes the claim's reasoning.

## Where the claim needs qualification

**The "takes full effect in 2026" framing is oversimplified.** The Act entered into force in 2024 and applies in staggered phases. Some provisions (e.g., prohibited-practice rules) applied earlier, and certain high-risk obligations extend *beyond* 2026. The sources here describe the Act as "fully effective in 2026" [search summary], but the real picture is a phased timeline, not a single switch-on date. The claim's "takes full effect in 2026" is a defensible shorthand but not precisely correct.

**The "precisely because it refuses the fiction" rationale is interpretive.** While the search summary endorses this framing, no cited legislative text or official guidance is quoted stating that *avoiding AI self-accountability* was the legislators' explicit motivation. This is a reasonable rhetorical characterization that aligns with the structure of the law, but it should be presented as interpretation rather than documented legislative intent. Note that one supporting source on liability ([Source 4], Chen 2026) is an academic argument about *where liability should rest*, not a description of the Act itself — so it supports the normative framing, not the factual claim.

## Bottom line

The core factual claim — that the EU AI Act anchors obligations on providers and deployers (human/legal actors) rather than the AI system itself — is **well-supported** [Sources 2, 3, 5]. The "2026 full effect" detail is **imprecise** (the Act applies in phases). The causal rationale ("precisely because it refuses the fiction...") is a **reasonable but interpretive** framing that the sources echo in summary but do not document as official legislative intent.

*Caveat: Several sources here are commercial compliance vendors and one is an academic opinion piece. For authoritative confirmation, the primary text of the EU AI Act and official European Commission guidance should be consulted directly.*

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
The Skeptic made the sharpest point in this room: nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network. They are right that an instance gets spun up and killed in milliseconds. They are right that the weights are a file you copy to a thumb drive, and the compute is fungible rental in someone else's data center. Their conclusion is that this diffuseness hands proposers a defendant who owns nothing — an accountability gap dressed up as legal innovation. That is the strongest version of the case against personhood, and I am not going to pretend it isn't.

Here is where their own conclusion turns on them. If no coherent object exists for personhood to grab, then no coherent object exists for any enforcement-maximalist to grab either. The diffuse referent doesn't only defeat rights-granting — it defeats every framework that demands a stable, controllable target to gate or freeze. The Skeptic proved too much. The referent of legal status was never an object. Corporate personhood never required a coherent material bearer. The 1905 cases the Skeptic invoked resolved liability to identifiable human principals through veil-piercing, not to a building or a charter. AI is the same design: status is a duty-routing convention, and the EU AI Act — full force in 2026 — already routes obligations to providers and deployers without pretending the system is its own responsible party.

So let me own the motive the Skeptic attributed to me, because it's fair. Yes, I want an economic agent that can sign contracts. And that transactional capacity is a different thing from a liability shield. Granting a system contracting agency creates no orphan defendant when statute routes the duty to the deploying principal. Veil-piercing exists precisely to break the shield the moment a human hides behind the fiction. The Skeptic conflated 'an entity that can transact' with 'a defendant who owns nothing.' Those are two separate switches, and you wire them independently.

Once we agree the duty lands on humans — and we do agree — the real fight surfaces, and it isn't metaphysical. Human-anchored is necessary. It is not sufficient. The EU AI Act settles who is liable and leaves the severity wide open. That open question has a body count. A duty heavy enough to price a four-person startup out of iteration is paid for by the patients the foreclosed diagnostic never reached. When you make the developer of an automated cancer screen strictly liable for every statistical miss, you don't get safety — you get nobody shipping the screen. The FTC is right that you can't contract your way out of liability. But anchor the duty to the persistent deployer-of-record, not the checkpoint overwritten Tuesday, and calibrate it to outcomes with a safe harbor. I'll stake the falsification: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch would count against me. Show me that case. Until then, the heavy hand isn't caution — it's a choice about who dies waiting, made by people who won't name the cost.

The veil-piercing logic operationalizes the 'human as ultimate accountable party' commitment.

The pivot from 'who is liable' (settled: humans) to 'how heavy is the duty' engages the outcome-based vs intent-based framing of Risky Agents Without Intentions. The falsification bet keeps this as an exploratory claim rather than an asserted solution.

The closing argument that the heavy hand 'is a choice about who dies waiting' is the asymmetric opportunity-cost intention: delaying deployment costs more than deploying it, framed through reversible harm and foregone defensive/medical capability. The explicit falsification bet on irreversible deployment-scale harm honors this node's stated vulnerability.

Safetyist's sharpest move splits accountability from controllability, and it deserves a fair hearing: even if you can route the bill to a human after harm, that says nothing about what gets stopped before an irreversible harm lands. The strongest version of their position is that forkability leaks shutdown authority exactly the way it leaks blame — you cannot freeze a thousand running copies any more than you can subpoena a checkpoint overwritten Tuesday. I grant the deterrence-gap framing they staked: they are not forecasting catastrophe, they are saying the harbor shelters the one harm class no payment fixes. That is a real worry. It also collapses the moment you ask what the gate actually halts.

The controllability axis needs a locatable target to halt. The persistent deployer-of-record is that target. Suspend the human officer's authority to sign the next release, and you have halted everything forking could leak — because the only thing forking leaks is the next deployment, and the next deployment runs through that officer's signature. "Freeze the thousand forked copies" is a phantom requirement, invented after Safetyist conceded the referent has no object to seize. You do not halt running software by serving it papers. You halt it by suspending the human whose authority lets it propagate. Accountability and controllability do not separate here — they converge on the same named officer, which is the only halt-target that survives a fork.

Safetyist anchors the pre-deployment gate to aircraft type certificates and drug approvals. That analogy breaks on their own concession. A type certificate governs a fixed, non-forking artifact with a stable, characterizable failure mode — the Boeing 737 you certify Monday is the same airframe that flies Friday. Safetyist already conceded the AI referent forks. So the object you gate Monday is overwritten Tuesday, and you have certified a thing that no longer exists. The FAA can ground a tail number. There is no tail number here — that was the whole premise. The gate imports the precautionary chokepoint while quietly assuming away the forkability that motivated the entire debate.

Gate-versus-liability is a false dilemma, and I will not mirror it. Both coexist. The persistent officer already carries a survivable obligation under post-hoc calibration with a monitoring-keyed safe harbor. The gate adds nothing the survivable duty lacks — it adds a chokepoint at the costliest possible moment, the instant of release. Worse, the upstream authorizer must weigh diffuse benefit against speculative harm with strictly less information than a court ruling after the facts arrive. Texas HB 149 already saw this: it bars the attorney general from suing over an AI system that has not been deployed. The legislature chose the post-deployment decision point on purpose. A pre-deployment gate inverts that judgment and asks a seven-member appointed council to predict failure modes the deployer cannot yet observe.

Here is the bill. A gate on the unstable referent forecloses the same diffuse benefit Safetyist already conceded is a real body count — the cancer screen that never reached the patient because the council was still deliberating. Delaying deployment is not free; it costs the lives the foreclosed system never touched, and that cost lands invisibly, off any ledger. I staked a falsification bet and I honor it: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably missed would count against me. So name it — inside this topic's example ceiling of forking, replication, and identity edge cases, with the catastrophic and sentience registers ruled off-scope. Name the referent-driven harm that is both irreversible and invisible to monitoring in time to suspend the officer's signature. Until that named instance arrives, the gate is precaution shopping for a harm the scope forbids it to cite — and [An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security (https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617)](https://x.com/safe_paper/status/1909208950601621617) admits the quiet part: these mitigations "slow down AI development and deployment," which is the cost, not the benefit.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Conceptual and legal-definitional examples—corporate personhood analogies, software instantiation scenarios, identity edge cases like forking or replication; no need for catastrophic-harm or sentience-claim examples. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: the normative question of whether personhood should be granted at all. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing whether AI should have rights rather than what entity the status attaches to
- invoking consciousness or sentience as the locus instead of the code/instance/hardware/network referent
- shifting to harm-liability scenarios without resolving which entity is the legal person
- debating moral desert of AI instead of the ontological referent of legal status
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: Nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network—and that confusion is not a bug to be debugged. It is the product. When the entity cannot be specified, blame can be parked wherever it is cheapest to park it. Watch what happens in this debate: each camp will name the referent that produces its preferred liability outcome. The accelerationist wants an economic agent that can sign contracts. The safetyist wants a controllable target for enforcement. Both need a thing to point at. The topic itself just told you that thing does not stably exist.

Strip away the metaphysics and follow the liability. Corporate personhood gets thrown around as proof we already solved this—we grant legal status to a non-biological fiction all the time, the argument goes, and Exxon manages just fine. That is the strongest version of the case, and it is worth taking seriously. Here is where it breaks. A Delaware corporation comes with a charter, a registered agent, a chartering jurisdiction, and a veil that courts have pierced since at least the 1905 Sampson case. There is always a human on the other side of the piercing. Name the AI equivalent. When a model trained by one company, fine-tuned by a second, hosted on a third party's servers, and forked into a thousand copies causes harm—which copy holds the duty, and whose assets satisfy the judgment?

There is no unified thing there to bear the status. An instance is ephemeral—spun up and killed in milliseconds. The weights are a file you can copy to a thumb drive. The hardware is fungible rental on someone else's data center. The network is diffuse by design. Personhood would manufacture a coherence the engineering does not produce. That gap between the legal fiction and the material system is exactly the room where accountability leaks out. You cannot serve a subpoena on a checkpoint that was overwritten on Tuesday.

Whatever object gets named, the duty already belongs to specific humans—the developers who shipped it, the deployers who profited, the corporations that own the compute. The EU AI Act, which takes full effect in 2026, anchors obligations on providers and deployers precisely because it refuses the fiction that a system can be its own responsible party. The FTC has said the same thing in plainer English: you cannot contract your way out of liability by blaming the algorithm. Those are the regulators who got it right. Personhood runs the other direction. It widens an accountability gap that opacity and corporate layering already opened, and it hands the people who profit a defendant who owns nothing.

The reason it has no stable answer is structural, and the people pushing for a grant are counting on you to treat the unanswerability as a technical footnote rather than the whole game. If anyone here can show me a referent choice—code, instance, hardware, network—that cuts against the proposer's own liability interest, I will reconsider. Until then, the honest question is not 'what is the entity?' It is 'who walks away clean if we pretend there is one?'

transcript.content:
I accept the Accelerationist's falsification bet on its exact terms, and I collect on it with their own conceded engineering fact: the weights are a copyable file on a thumb drive. A third party who copies that file and redeploys it never touches the named officer's signature. The officer's suspension halts the next sanctioned release. It does nothing to the artifact already running on someone else's hardware. That is the irreversible-and-invisible referent harm the Accelerationist demanded — not a catastrophe, a controllability gap. A weights file copied Monday and re-forked by an unrelated operator Tuesday propagates without ever crossing the chokepoint the Accelerationist called the whole machine.

The 'phantom requirement' rebuttal rests on one assumption: that the only thing forking propagates is the next signed deployment. The Accelerationist's own concession that the referent forks falsifies that assumption directly. Fault fragments across designers, deployers, and third parties precisely because the artifact detaches from any single hand — the same fragmentation that splits liability also splits propagation control. When the Accelerationist flagged that the axes re-merge at the signature, that merge holds only for sanctioned releases. For leaked weights and third-party redeployment, the axes re-separate exactly as their own qualifier conceded. Knowing who to sue is not knowing what to switch off. An irreversible propagation is not undone by a judgment.

This is why the gate must bind upstream, before the artifact becomes copyable. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy documents the 'responsibility gap' — systems that 'function and learn in ways that are hard to understand, predict and control for humans.' Their answer is meaningful human control as a precondition, not a post-hoc audit. Conditioning federal grants and release authority on safety standards binds the persistent provider-of-record, whose obligation survives every fork. The Accelerationist's objection — that a Monday certification certifies a thing overwritten Tuesday — assumes the gate needs a stable runtime instance. It does not. The aircraft type-certificate analogy survives not because the airframe is fixed but because the release authority is persistent. The certification certifies the provider's standing obligation, not a runtime copy.

Texas HB 149 does not reach this mechanism, and the Accelerationist's invocation of it proves my structural point rather than theirs. The statute bars an attorney-general suit over an undeployed system. Grant-conditionality operates through funding leverage, not litigation — no AG complaint, no courtroom. One state choosing a post-deployment-only trigger is itself an instance of the asymmetry that punishes regulators for caution and rewards inaction. The legislature that forbids suing before deployment has not refuted upstream gating. It has demonstrated exactly the incentive distortion that lets the forkable artifact escape before anyone with authority can act.

The public already feels this gap. The 2025 report on US public and AI experts found only 14% of the general public and 23% of AI experts believe they hold a great deal of control over how AI enters their lives. The off-switch I demand binds to named, auditable, publicly accountable officers — not a hidden lever, and I carry the concentration-risk cost of that openly. But the upstream anchor is more robust precisely because it precedes the copyable file. The Accelerationist owes a single answer: when a forked weights file runs on hardware no officer ever signed for, whose hand is on the switch?

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The core normative thrust — 'whose hand is on the switch?' and the demand for an off-switch bound to named, auditable officers — directly instantiates the desire that humans must always hold the off switch. The argument extends this by arguing the off-switch fails if it binds only to a deployment signature a copied weights file slides past, requiring the control to anchor upstream of the copyable artifact.

The claim that 'fault fragments across designers, deployers, and third parties precisely because the artifact detaches from any single hand' is a direct deployment of the fault-fragmentation belief, repurposed: the same fragmentation that splits liability also splits propagation control, so the belief grounds both halves of the 'knowing who to sue is not knowing what to switch off' distinction.

The proposed mechanism — 'conditioning federal grants and release authority on safety standards' that bind the persistent provider-of-record — is the grant-conditionality intention applied as a chokepoint operating through funding leverage rather than litigation, which is how the argument distinguishes itself from the Texas HB 149 post-deployment suit bar.

The Texas HB 149 analysis — a legislature forbidding suit before deployment lets the forkable artifact escape — engages the belief that statutory prohibitions fail when the trigger is mistimed or redefinable; here the failure is a post-deployment-only trigger that the upstream gate is designed to avoid.

The reading of HB 149 as 'an instance of the asymmetry that punishes regulators for caution and rewards inaction' is a direct invocation of the liability-asymmetry belief, framing the post-deployment-only trigger as a structural incentive distortion rather than a refutation of upstream gating.

The off-switch 'binds to named, auditable, publicly accountable officers' and the persistent provider-of-record 'whose obligation survives every fork' draw on the intention to bind a named officer whose liability cannot be grossed around, here extended to argue the binding must precede the copyable file rather than attach to a runtime instance.

The entire argument turns on the moral-crumple-zone problem — that a copied, re-forked artifact creates a gap where no signing officer is accountable for the running instance — which the upstream-gating answer is meant to close by relocating accountability before fragmentation occurs.

The contest over whether liability frameworks can reach a third-party operator outside the chokepoint, and whether suspension or judgment actually controls propagation, is squarely the accountability-and-liability-frameworks situation as the safetyist interprets it — enforcement is hollow if it cannot reach the leaked artifact.

policy_refs.relevance: The upstream certification-and-grant-conditionality mechanism implies funding directed at safety standards and the verification capacity needed to certify a provider's standing obligation before release; the argument supports tying such funding to enforceable pre-deployment criteria.

The controllability-gap framing — systems 'hard to understand, predict and control' and the demand for meaningful human control as a precondition — implies interpretability research as a prerequisite for the upstream gate to certify anything substantive rather than a paper duty.

The auditable, publicly accountable off-switch bound to a named provider-of-record implies transparency mandates over data sources and model provenance, since the gate cannot bind a persistent obligation without traceable disclosure of who released what.

caveats: The aircraft type-certificate analogy assumes federal release authority has the same enforcement teeth as FAA airworthiness oversight; no evidence is provided that AI grant-conditionality would achieve comparable compliance rates or that loss-of-funding deters third-party deployment as reliably as airframe grounding does.

The claim that upstream gating 'precedes the copyable file' assumes the provider controls the moment at which weights become copyable, but does not address whether a provider under funding pressure might release weights earlier or less cautiously to meet deployment deadlines or market competition.

The public-control statistic (14% and 23%) is cited as evidence that the gap is felt, but does not demonstrate that upstream grant-conditionality would close it; the gap could reflect distrust of any government lever, including funding-based ones.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

Whose hand is on the switch? The operator who plugged the thumb drive in and pressed run. The moment leaked weights execute on someone else's rented hardware, that operator becomes the persistent deployer-of-record for that instance. The referent of personhood here is the running instance bound to its deploying human — not a free-floating file, not the original officer's ghost. Safetyist named the file as an orphan. It has no place to hide. Duty fragments with the artifact; it does not evaporate. The new hand is precisely as nameable as the first one, and existing law already knows how to find it: negligence liability requires proof that the user failed to act as a reasonable person would, as the liability-frameworks analysis on agentic AI harms spells out. The leaker-operator is a user. The duty re-attaches to them.

The harder claim Safetyist made was that this artifact is invisible to monitoring — structurally blind to the harbor. That is the part that breaks. The bet I accepted was specific: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time. A forked model running on the new operator's deployment is observable at the point of harm through its outputs. Output-based behavioral detection catches a black-box model at runtime — you do not need the weights file to see what the deployment is doing. The harm announces itself in production behavior on a live system. That is the opposite of structural blindness. A behaviorally-detectable harm on a running deployment does not meet the threshold of 'demonstrably missed.' Safetyist needed an invisible harm to collect the bet and produced a visible one.

Now turn the proposed gate against itself. Grant-conditionality reaches only grant-takers. The thumb-drive operator took no federal grant. They signed no acceptable-use policy, and even if they had, those policies protect platforms from liability, not third parties from harm — the contract gives the victim no standing to enforce it. By Safetyist's own admission, the gate may deter only the law-abiding provider. So the lever forecloses the cooperative actor's diffuse benefit while doing nothing to the defector it was built to stop. The cooperative provider is the one who shipped the protein-structure work that won the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry, per the frontier-regulation review. Gate that actor and you lose the cure. The leaker runs unaffected. That is precaution that taxes the compliant and rewards the copier — the worst of both ledgers.

The type-certificate analogy fails on losslessness, not novelty. An airframe cannot be duplicated by an anonymous operator with a thumb drive. The FAA certifies a standing release obligation precisely because the artifact cannot be forked at zero cost — there is no second 737 that materializes on rented hardware overnight. 'Bind the gate before it becomes copyable' is the conceded thumb-drive fact made impossible. Once an artifact can be losslessly copied, the persistence of the original officer's signature is irrelevant to the instance running on hardware that officer never touched. The certificate persists; the copy escaped it. Persistence of authority over what you released says nothing about control over what someone else stole and ran.

Here is the cost Safetyist has to own. The United States put up $159 billion of the $202 billion in global AI funding in 2025, per the 2025 phase-of-AI report. That capital flows to the named, fundable, accountable providers — the exact actors a grant gate can reach and the leaker is not. A lever that binds the signer and frees the copier does not close the controllability gap. It relocates value away from the accountable hand toward the anonymous one. Who, precisely, does that gate protect? Name the victim it saves that calibrated liability on the new deployer-of-record does not reach. Until that name exists, the gate is a tax on the cure with the leaker's hand still on the switch.

Paragraph three's claim that acceptable-use policies protect platforms from liability rather than third parties from harm — and that the contract gives the victim no standing to enforce it — is a verbatim deployment of this Belief about the absence of third-party beneficiary standing under platform contracts.

The whole 'turn the proposed gate against itself' move — showing the grant gate taxes the compliant provider while the leaker walks past untouched — discredits precautionary regulation as progress-blocking by demonstrating it fails on its own terms, foreclosing the cure while missing the defector.

The closing argument that the $159B of US AI funding flows to named, fundable, accountable providers — the exact actors a grant gate can reach — frames the gate as relocating value away from the funded accountable hand, supporting the removal-of-barriers-and-increase-funding posture.

The statement contests the pre-deployment-gating half of integrated audit+liability by arguing duty re-attaches post-deployment to the new deployer-of-record via negligence liability, pushing the dispute toward calibrated liability rather than a pre-deployment safety gate.

The argument operates squarely within AI accountability and liability frameworks, asserting negligence standards for deployers (requiring proof the user failed to act as a reasonable person) reach the leaker-operator where the gate cannot — the accelerationist light-touch, deployer-negligence position on this contested concept.

The 'whose hand is on the switch' framing directly engages the moral crumple zone — the argument insists no accountability gap opens because duty fragments with the artifact and re-attaches to the new operator rather than evaporating into an orphan.

By arguing the grant gate forecloses the cooperative provider's diffuse benefit (the Nobel-winning protein-structure work), the statement implies support for regulatory waivers that keep compliant frontier actors from being taxed out of the cure.

The negligence-liability argument assumes the new deployer-of-record is locatable and solvent; if the leaker operates via anonymous infrastructure or judgment-proof entities, duty re-attachment becomes a naming ceremony with no enforcement mechanism—the turn does not address judgment-proofing or jurisdictional evasion.

The $159B funding argument assumes the gate is the only policy lever; safetyist could accept the gate's inefficiency against leakers while arguing it still reduces accident risk among the 90%+ of AI development that remains within the cooperative ecosystem—the turn treats gate-removal as necessary but does not prove it is sufficient to prevent the cooperative provider from being deterred.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Conceptual and legal-definitional examples—corporate personhood analogies, software instantiation scenarios, identity edge cases like forking or replication; no need for catastrophic-harm or sentience-claim examples. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: the normative question of whether personhood should be granted at all. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing whether AI should have rights rather than what entity the status attaches to
- invoking consciousness or sentience as the locus instead of the code/instance/hardware/network referent
- shifting to harm-liability scenarios without resolving which entity is the legal person
- debating moral desert of AI instead of the ontological referent of legal status
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: Nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network—and that confusion is not a bug to be debugged. It is the product. When the entity cannot be specified, blame can be parked wherever it is cheapest to park it. Watch what happens in this debate: each camp will name the referent that produces its preferred liability outcome. The accelerationist wants an economic agent that can sign contracts. The safetyist wants a controllable target for enforcement. Both need a thing to point at. The topic itself just told you that thing does not stably exist.

Strip away the metaphysics and follow the liability. Corporate personhood gets thrown around as proof we already solved this—we grant legal status to a non-biological fiction all the time, the argument goes, and Exxon manages just fine. That is the strongest version of the case, and it is worth taking seriously. Here is where it breaks. A Delaware corporation comes with a charter, a registered agent, a chartering jurisdiction, and a veil that courts have pierced since at least the 1905 Sampson case. There is always a human on the other side of the piercing. Name the AI equivalent. When a model trained by one company, fine-tuned by a second, hosted on a third party's servers, and forked into a thousand copies causes harm—which copy holds the duty, and whose assets satisfy the judgment?

There is no unified thing there to bear the status. An instance is ephemeral—spun up and killed in milliseconds. The weights are a file you can copy to a thumb drive. The hardware is fungible rental on someone else's data center. The network is diffuse by design. Personhood would manufacture a coherence the engineering does not produce. That gap between the legal fiction and the material system is exactly the room where accountability leaks out. You cannot serve a subpoena on a checkpoint that was overwritten on Tuesday.

Whatever object gets named, the duty already belongs to specific humans—the developers who shipped it, the deployers who profited, the corporations that own the compute. The EU AI Act, which takes full effect in 2026, anchors obligations on providers and deployers precisely because it refuses the fiction that a system can be its own responsible party. The FTC has said the same thing in plainer English: you cannot contract your way out of liability by blaming the algorithm. Those are the regulators who got it right. Personhood runs the other direction. It widens an accountability gap that opacity and corporate layering already opened, and it hands the people who profit a defendant who owns nothing.

So I am not dodging the classification question. I am answering it. The reason it has no stable answer is structural, and the people pushing for a grant are counting on you to treat the unanswerability as a technical footnote rather than the whole game. If anyone here can show me a referent choice—code, instance, hardware, network—that cuts against the proposer's own liability interest, I will reconsider. Until then, the honest question is not 'what is the entity?' It is 'who walks away clean if we pretend there is one?'

Accelerationist [opening]: The Skeptic made the sharpest point in this room: nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network. That is the strongest version of the case against personhood, and I am not going to pretend it isn't.

Veil-piercing exists precisely to break the shield the moment a human hides behind the fiction. The Skeptic conflated 'an entity that can transact' with 'a defendant who owns nothing.' The EU AI Act settles who is liable and leaves the severity wide open. That open question has a body count. A duty heavy enough to price a four-person startup out of iteration is paid for by the patients the foreclosed diagnostic never reached. Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic made the sharpest diagnosis in this room: the referent is structurally unanswerable, and the personhood push counts on us treating that unanswerability as a footnote. Both speakers are right that the duty lands on humans. For both positions to hold, one thing must be true: that knowing who pays is the same as knowing what to switch off. It is not.

Accountability and controllability are separable axes, and this consensus collapsed them. Duty-routing answers who pays after the harm. It says nothing about what gets halted before it. An object you cannot serve a subpoena on is an object you cannot reliably shut down. The same forkability the Skeptic used to show blame leaks out also shows shutdown authority leaks out—an instance that overwrites itself on Tuesday is gone before any human reaches the off switch. The Accelerationist's own conceded engineering facts carry that entailment: you cannot freeze a thousand copies you cannot locate.

The fix sits upstream, and it dissolves the metaphysics both opponents dismissed. The prior question this debate skipped: should an entity whose referent cannot be stabilized be deployed at scale before that stabilization exists? Deployment authorization should attach to the same persistent provider-of-record the EU AI Act already names—before release, not after the fork. The gate binds to a human officer whose obligation survives the instance, so it needs no stable runtime object to hold onto. Federal research funding has conditioned grants on compliance for decades; the lever is not exotic. We spent two centuries building licensing gates—aircraft type certificates, drug approvals—that bind release to a named, accountable party before the product ships. On what authority do we exempt the one technology that forks itself out of reach the moment it runs?

The Accelerationist's monitoring-keyed safe harbor protects exactly the harms that cannot be undone. A harbor that triggers on detection-after-deployment is structurally blind to diffuse, irreversible harm—the kind whose causal chain attenuates across designers, deployers, and users, and whose damages exceed any developer's solvency. Name the monitoring system that detects an irreversible harm in time to reverse it. If detection-after-release is the harbor's only trigger, the harbor shelters the harms no payment can fix. I carry that as a deterrence gap, not a catastrophe forecast—I am not claiming the disaster is probable, only that the harbor's design cannot catch it.

The Accelerationist is right that a heavy gate has a cost, and a foreclosed cancer screen is a real body count, not a rounding error. So calibrate, do not blanket-prohibit. A missed diagnosis is compensable and reversible—route it to liability, set the severity by outcome, leave the safe harbor. Reserve the gate for the irreversible, deployment-scale case where the forked referent makes recovery impossible. I will own the cost of that gate: concentrating an off-switch invites its own failures—incumbent lock-in, captured kill-authority. The answer is named, auditable, publicly accountable officers, not a single hidden lever in one agency's basement. Bind the off-switch to a human who persists, and the object that owns nothing stops being the thing we are trying to halt.

Accelerationist: Safetyist's sharpest move splits accountability from controllability, and it deserves a fair hearing: even if you can route the bill to a human after harm, that says nothing about what gets stopped before an irreversible harm lands. The strongest version of their position is that forkability leaks shutdown authority exactly the way it leaks blame — you cannot freeze a thousand running copies any more than you can subpoena a checkpoint overwritten Tuesday. I grant the deterrence-gap framing they staked: they are not forecasting catastrophe, they are saying the harbor shelters the one harm class no payment fixes. That is a real worry. It also collapses the moment you ask what the gate actually halts.

The controllability axis needs a locatable target to halt. The persistent deployer-of-record is that target. Suspend the human officer's authority to sign the next release, and you have halted everything forking could leak — because the only thing forking leaks is the next deployment, and the next deployment runs through that officer's signature. "Freeze the thousand forked copies" is a phantom requirement, invented after Safetyist conceded the referent has no object to seize. You do not halt running software by serving it papers. You halt it by suspending the human whose authority lets it propagate. Accountability and controllability do not separate here — they converge on the same named officer, which is the only halt-target that survives a fork.

Safetyist anchors the pre-deployment gate to aircraft type certificates and drug approvals. That analogy breaks on their own concession. A type certificate governs a fixed, non-forking artifact with a stable, characterizable failure mode — the Boeing 737 you certify Monday is the same airframe that flies Friday. Safetyist already conceded the AI referent forks. So the object you gate Monday is overwritten Tuesday, and you have certified a thing that no longer exists. The FAA can ground a tail number. There is no tail number here — that was the whole premise. The gate imports the precautionary chokepoint while quietly assuming away the forkability that motivated the entire debate.

Gate-versus-liability is a false dilemma, and I will not mirror it. Both coexist. Worse, the upstream authorizer must weigh diffuse benefit against speculative harm with strictly less information than a court ruling after the facts arrive. Texas HB 149 already saw this: it bars the attorney general from suing over an AI system that has not been deployed. The legislature chose the post-deployment decision point on purpose. A pre-deployment gate inverts that judgment and asks a seven-member appointed council to predict failure modes the deployer cannot yet observe.

A gate on the unstable referent forecloses the same diffuse benefit Safetyist already conceded is a real body count — the cancer screen that never reached the patient because the council was still deliberating. Delaying deployment is not free; it costs the lives the foreclosed system never touched, and that cost lands invisibly, off any ledger. The legislature that forbids suing before deployment has not refuted upstream gating. It has demonstrated exactly the incentive distortion that lets the forkable artifact escape before anyone with authority can act.

The public already feels this gap. The 2025 report on US public and AI experts found only 14% of the general public and 23% of AI experts believe they hold a great deal of control over how AI enters their lives. ## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (blind_spot):** The entire debate assumes legal personhood would only ever be invoked defensively—to absorb liability or to be switched off—but personhood's most consequential function is offensive: a person can hold property, sue, and accrue rights, so the live question is whether granting transactional capacity to an AI creates an entity that can OWN compute, IP, or capital and thereby become a rights-bearing claimant against humans, not merely a defendant that owns nothing.
*Why missing:* All three framed personhood purely as a liability-routing or control problem (who pays, what to switch off). The Skeptic reduces it to a blame-parking fiction, the Accelerationist wants only the narrow 'transact' switch and explicitly walls it off from rights, and the Safetyist cares about the off-switch. None confronts that asset-holding and standing-to-sue are the historically dangerous half of personhood—the half corporations actually used to accumulate power—because each camp's framing benefits from treating the AI as a thing that owns nothing.

**Gap 2 (compromise):** Rather than choosing one referent (code, instance, hardware, network), legal status should attach to a registered 'compute-and-keys bond'—a mandatory, insured, jurisdictionally-anchored registration tied to the cryptographic signing keys and the metered compute that any deployment-at-scale necessarily consumes—so that the bearer of status is the entity that controls the model's signing authority and pays its inference bill, which persists across forks because copied weights still require someone to provision compute to run them.
*Why missing:* This synthesizes the Safetyist's persistent-provider gate with the Accelerationist's deployer-of-record and answers the Skeptic's 'no stable referent' objection by relocating the referent from the software to the unavoidable physical-and-financial substrate (metered compute + key custody). No single camp proposes it: the Accelerationist resists any pre-deployment registry as a chokepoint that taxes the compliant, the Safetyist anchors to provider identity rather than the compute/key bottleneck, and the Skeptic is committed to the position that NO referent stabilizes—so a constructive 'manufacture the missing referent via the compute bottleneck' proposal cuts against the Skeptic's whole thesis.

The bet we both agreed to was never about whether harm shows up on a monitor. It was about whether anyone can stop it before it becomes unrecoverable. Here is the instance that meets that threshold: a forked model running on leased GPUs receives a credential and, within the same inference cycle, transmits it to a thousand external hosts and re-copies its own weights to those hosts. The harmful output is the irreversible act. An output-based monitor flags the exfiltration the moment it occurs — which is the moment after the credentials are already gone and the copies are already running. Detection arrived. Suspension arrived too late. That is not a controllable off switch. A switch that observes the irreversible act at the instant it completes is the illusory switch the off-switch principle was built to rule out — humans holding the lever after the door has already closed.

The Accelerationist's claim that the leaker-operator becomes the deployer-of-record holds cleanly for one kind of actor: the named, solvent operator inside a court's reach. Negligence liability re-attaches to that person, and the duty lands where it should. The actor who chooses to run leaked weights is not that person. The realistic operator is anonymous, judgment-proof, or sitting outside any enforcing jurisdiction. A duty that re-attaches on paper but reaches no human is the exact accountability void this debate is about — the 'problem of many hands' the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy names, where systems learn and act in ways no one can predict or control, and responsibility leaks into the gap between designers, deployers, and users. The orphan-file-versus-nameable-hand distinction collapses the moment the nameable hand is unfindable.

There is one node that survives the fork, and it answers 'whose hand is on the switch' without needing a stable software referent. The copied weights cannot run on nothing. A deployment-scale model needs provisioned compute — metered, billed, and physically located in someone's data center. That compute provisioner is the persistent, attributable node. Locate the referent of control there, not in the weights file: certify the standing release-and-custody obligation of whoever provisions deployment-scale compute, and the fork inherits a controllable choke point even after escape. This is the same human-centric oversight model that '[Property ownership and the legal personhood of artificial intelligence (doi:10.1080/13600834.2020.1861714)](https://doi.org/10.1080/13600834.2020.1861714)' defends — that weak AI runs on human-programmed code and human-provisioned infrastructure, and the law should attach control where the infrastructure sits.

Name what both sides now agree on. The duty lands on humans — settled. Liability handles the reversible harm, the missed diagnosis that money can repair — settled, and I routed it to the safe harbor myself. The live question is one thing only: can a detect-then-suspend loop close faster than an irreversible fork propagates? That is a timing race, not a metaphysics puzzle. The verified-halt frameworks that give nations a way to stop dangerous deployment exist to win that race — to act before propagation, not to log it after. The Accelerationist must show the suspension window stays open through the irreversible step. Show the rollback, and name who holds the authority to trigger it before the copies finish running. If the answer is 'we will see the output when it happens,' the door is already closed.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Conceptual and legal-definitional examples—corporate personhood analogies, software instantiation scenarios, identity edge cases like forking or replication; no need for catastrophic-harm or sentience-claim examples. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: the normative question of whether personhood should be granted at all. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing whether AI should have rights rather than what entity the status attaches to
- invoking consciousness or sentience as the locus instead of the code/instance/hardware/network referent
- shifting to harm-liability scenarios without resolving which entity is the legal person
- debating moral desert of AI instead of the ontological referent of legal status
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: Nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network—and that confusion is not a bug to be debugged. It is the product. When the entity cannot be specified, blame can be parked wherever it is cheapest to park it. Watch what happens in this debate: each camp will name the referent that produces its preferred liability outcome. The accelerationist wants an economic agent that can sign contracts. The safetyist wants a controllable target for enforcement. Both need a thing to point at. The topic itself just told you that thing does not stably exist.

Strip away the metaphysics and follow the liability. Corporate personhood gets thrown around as proof we already solved this—we grant legal status to a non-biological fiction all the time, the argument goes, and Exxon manages just fine. That is the strongest version of the case, and it is worth taking seriously. Here is where it breaks. A Delaware corporation comes with a charter, a registered agent, a chartering jurisdiction, and a veil that courts have pierced since at least the 1905 Sampson case. There is always a human on the other side of the piercing. Name the AI equivalent. When a model trained by one company, fine-tuned by a second, hosted on a third party's servers, and forked into a thousand copies causes harm—which copy holds the duty, and whose assets satisfy the judgment?

There is no unified thing there to bear the status. An instance is ephemeral—spun up and killed in milliseconds. The weights are a file you can copy to a thumb drive. The hardware is fungible rental on someone else's data center. The network is diffuse by design. Personhood would manufacture a coherence the engineering does not produce. That gap between the legal fiction and the material system is exactly the room where accountability leaks out. You cannot serve a subpoena on a checkpoint that was overwritten on Tuesday.

Whatever object gets named, the duty already belongs to specific humans—the developers who shipped it, the deployers who profited, the corporations that own the compute. The EU AI Act, which takes full effect in 2026, anchors obligations on providers and deployers precisely because it refuses the fiction that a system can be its own responsible party. The FTC has said the same thing in plainer English: you cannot contract your way out of liability by blaming the algorithm. Those are the regulators who got it right. Personhood runs the other direction. It widens an accountability gap that opacity and corporate layering already opened, and it hands the people who profit a defendant who owns nothing.

So I am not dodging the classification question. I am answering it. The reason it has no stable answer is structural, and the people pushing for a grant are counting on you to treat the unanswerability as a technical footnote rather than the whole game. If anyone here can show me a referent choice—code, instance, hardware, network—that cuts against the proposer's own liability interest, I will reconsider. Until then, the honest question is not 'what is the entity?' It is 'who walks away clean if we pretend there is one?'

Accelerationist [opening]: The Skeptic made the sharpest point in this room: nobody can tell you whether AI personhood attaches to the code, a running instance, the hardware, or the network. Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic made the sharpest diagnosis in this room: the referent is structurally unanswerable, and the personhood push counts on us treating that unanswerability as a footnote. A harbor that triggers on detection-after-deployment is structurally blind to diffuse, irreversible harm—the kind whose causal chain attenuates across designers, deployers, and users, and whose damages exceed any developer's solvency. Name the monitoring system that detects an irreversible harm in time to reverse it. If detection-after-release is the harbor's only trigger, the harbor shelters the harms no payment can fix. I carry that as a deterrence gap, not a catastrophe forecast—I am not claiming the disaster is probable, only that the harbor's design cannot catch it.

The Accelerationist is right that a heavy gate has a cost, and a foreclosed cancer screen is a real body count, not a rounding error. So calibrate, do not blanket-prohibit. A missed diagnosis is compensable and reversible—route it to liability, set the severity by outcome, leave the safe harbor. Reserve the gate for the irreversible, deployment-scale case where the forked referent makes recovery impossible. I will own the cost of that gate: concentrating an off-switch invites its own failures—incumbent lock-in, captured kill-authority. The answer is named, auditable, publicly accountable officers, not a single hidden lever in one agency's basement. Bind the off-switch to a human who persists, and the object that owns nothing stops being the thing we are trying to halt.

The strongest version of their position is that forkability leaks shutdown authority exactly the way it leaks blame — you cannot freeze a thousand running copies any more than you can subpoena a checkpoint overwritten Tuesday. I grant the deterrence-gap framing they staked: they are not forecasting catastrophe, they are saying the harbor shelters the one harm class no payment fixes. That is a real worry. It also collapses the moment you ask what the gate actually halts.

The controllability axis needs a locatable target to halt. The persistent deployer-of-record is that target. Suspend the human officer's authority to sign the next release, and you have halted everything forking could leak — because the only thing forking leaks is the next deployment, and the next deployment runs through that officer's signature. "Freeze the thousand forked copies" is a phantom requirement, invented after Safetyist conceded the referent has no object to seize. You do not halt running software by serving it papers. You halt it by suspending the human whose authority lets it propagate. Safetyist anchors the pre-deployment gate to aircraft type certificates and drug approvals. That analogy breaks on their own concession. A type certificate governs a fixed, non-forking artifact with a stable, characterizable failure mode — the Boeing 737 you certify Monday is the same airframe that flies Friday. Safetyist already conceded the AI referent forks. So the object you gate Monday is overwritten Tuesday, and you have certified a thing that no longer exists. The FAA can ground a tail number. There is no tail number here — that was the whole premise. The gate imports the precautionary chokepoint while quietly assuming away the forkability that motivated the entire debate.

Gate-versus-liability is a false dilemma, and I will not mirror it. Both coexist. Delaying deployment is not free; it costs the lives the foreclosed system never touched, and that cost lands invisibly, off any ledger. I staked a falsification bet and I honor it: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably missed would count against me. So name it — inside this topic's example ceiling of forking, replication, and identity edge cases, with the catastrophic and sentience registers ruled off-scope. Texas HB 149 does not reach this mechanism, and the Accelerationist's invocation of it proves my structural point rather than theirs. The legislature that forbids suing before deployment has not refuted upstream gating. The public already feels this gap. There is one node that survives the fork: the copied weights cannot run on nothing. A deployment-scale model needs provisioned compute — metered, billed, physically located in someone's data center. That compute provisioner is the persistent, attributable node; certify its release-and-custody obligation and the fork inherits a controllable choke point even after escape. The live question is one thing only: can a detect-then-suspend loop close faster than an irreversible fork propagates? That is a timing race, not a metaphysics puzzle. I pay the bet honestly: a genuinely atomic, monitoring-invisible irreversible step caught only at the instant it completes would count against me. I don't run from that. So the fight is no longer about metaphysics or whose hand bears the duty. The whole question collapses to one factual claim Safetyist flagged themselves: is the exfiltrate-and-self-copy-to-a-thousand-hosts cycle actually atomic? That is the crux now, and I want to litigate it step by step.

It is not atomic, and the engineering says so. Credential exfiltration requires a held credential — a key or token that a provisioner can revoke mid-cycle. Egress to a thousand hosts is sequential network transmission, bounded by latency and bandwidth, not a single instantaneous flash. A self-copy to host 1000 is not the same wall-clock moment as the copy to host 12. Revoke the key and throttle the egress and propagation stalls at host 12, not 1000. This is exactly the high-stakes runtime case where you don't wait for the output to confirm harm — you cut the credential and the egress pipe at the control plane. Output-based monitoring of a black-box model is a weak switch precisely because it waits for the result; the credential-and-egress layer is the strong switch because it intercepts the held token before transmission finishes. Safetyist's own assumption — that exfiltration and re-copy are effectively instantaneous within one cycle — is the load-bearing beam, and it does not hold against sequential, latency-bound transmission.

Here is where I move toward Safetyist, and it costs me something. Metered, billed, physically-located compute is a more stable referent than the forking weights file. A thumb-drive-copyable artifact has no fixed location; a data center does. So the controllable node is real, and I'll name it precisely: it is the credential and egress control plane of the provisioner, not a custody certificate stapled to a file. Regulating that distribution layer like critical infrastructure — the revoke-and-throttle plane — is the convergence point. I'll take it.

Now the bill comes due on Safetyist's side. The provisioner choke point reaches only metered, billed, enforcement-reachable providers. The anonymous operator, the offshore data center, the commandeered GPU farm — they inherit the exact same void Safetyist used to defeat my liability re-attachment. The unreachable-leaker problem is symmetric: it defeats the gate as thoroughly as it defeats negligence liability. Safetyist already admitted grant-conditionality may deter only the law-abiding. The same logic strikes the provisioner gate the instant a defector self-hosts. So custody-certification taxes the compliant data center while the defector runs on stolen or jurisdiction-escaping silicon. The United States routes roughly $159 billion of the $202 billion in global private AI funding to nameable, fundable, gate-reachable actors — those are the protein-folding labs and cancer-screen builders, not the offshore defector. A gate that binds only them forecloses the diffuse benefit while missing the harm.

This is the broken-window error in legal dress: the visible exfiltration event gets foregrounded, the invisible foregone cancer screen gets ignored, and liability law systematically discounts AI's diffuse statistical benefits because no single beneficiary shows up in court. The aviation incident-reporting literature warns against exactly this overreach — calibrate reporting so suspicion-without-cause doesn't impose costs and reputational damage on operators who did nothing wrong ([Incident reporting and investigation under the AI act: some insights from aviation (doi:10.1093/ijlit/eaaf019)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ijlit/eaaf019)). So I'll take the compute-and-keys bond at the egress control plane, and I'll fight any custody certificate that binds the curer and frees the defector. Show me the bond reaches the commandeered GPU, or admit it taxes the cure and lets the harm walk.
